planting.note: Divide congested clumps of small bulbs or plant nursery starts in spring in gritty, fast-draining potting mix or sandy garden soil in bright light; silver squill multiplies readily from offset bulbs that form dense colonies at the soil surface.

directions: Divide congested clumps of bulbs or plant nursery starts in spring in gritty, fast-draining potting mix in bright indirect light to partial sun, since this small South African bulb is grown chiefly as a foliage and container plant rather than for its flowers. The fleshy, lance-shaped leaves are marbled silver-gray over green with a glossy sheen and flushed purple underneath, forming a dense, spreading colony as the bulbs multiply just above or at the soil surface. Short spikes of small, greenish flowers with reflexed purple tips appear in spring but are secondary to the striking foliage display. Allow the soil to dry between waterings and protect from frost, since silver squill stores water in its leaves and bulbs like a succulent and rots quickly in cold, soggy conditions; it thrives as a houseplant, hanging basket subject, or groundcover in frost-free gardens.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in very well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; keep completely dry through summer dormancy to prevent rot.

directions: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in very well-drained, sandy soil in full sun, then let the plant grow undisturbed through the cool winter months. Wine cups is one of the most striking of the Cape's winter-rainfall baboon flowers, producing short, pleated fans of hairy leaves and low sprays of small, cup-shaped flowers whose outer tepals are a deep, velvety wine-red that shades abruptly into an electric violet-blue at the petal tips, a two-tone combination unlike almost anything else in the spring bulb world. Flowers open low among the foliage in late winter to early spring and are followed by complete summer dormancy, during which the corms must be kept bone dry to avoid rot. Because the flowers sit close to the ground and are easily missed in a mixed border, wine cups is best appreciated in a raised bed, trough, or pot near a path where its unusual coloring can be seen up close.

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in very well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; the densely hairy leaves and stems are a hallmark of the species and help distinguish it from other babianas even before flowering.

directions: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in very well-drained, sandy soil in full sun, allowing the plant to grow through the cool, wet Cape winter and bloom in early to mid spring. Red baboon flower is instantly recognizable by the dense covering of soft white hairs on its pleated, fan-like leaves and flower stems, a texture that gives the whole plant a silvery, felted look before the rich, velvety crimson-to-magenta flowers with darker nectar guides open in loose spikes. Like other Cape babianas, it needs a strictly dry summer dormancy to survive from one season to the next, so it is best grown in a pot that can be kept dry and shaded once the foliage yellows, or in a raised bed with sharp drainage where no summer irrigation reaches the corms. Its intense flower color and unusual hairy texture make it a favorite among specialist bulb collectors growing a broader palette of South African corms.

planting.note: Plant large bulbs with the neck at or just below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; unlike most Albuca species, this one is evergreen and appreciates regular moisture rather than a strict dry dormancy.

directions: Plant large bulbs with the neck at or just below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in spring, or grow year-round in a large container in colder areas. Nelson's albuca is among the largest and toughest of the South African albucas, forming a substantial, evergreen rosette of broad, strappy, dark-green leaves from a bulb that can reach the size of a large onion, and sending up a stout flower spike two to three feet tall crowned with dozens of pendent, waxy, white, star-shaped flowers, each petal marked with a central green-and-maroon stripe on the outside. Native to the summer-rainfall grasslands of KwaZulu-Natal and the Eastern Cape, it tolerates regular garden watering and heavier soils far better than the winter-growing, dry-dormant albucas from the Cape, making it a much easier, more forgiving landscape and container plant. Established clumps bloom reliably in late spring to summer and can remain undisturbed and evergreen for years in frost-free gardens, or be brought indoors as a large potted specimen where winters are cold.

common_name: Giant Wedding Iris (Lord Howe Island Iris)

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun with shelter from strong wind; this is by far the largest Dietes species and needs considerable room to reach mature size.

directions: Plant container-grown divisions in rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, sheltered from strong wind, and allow several years for clumps to reach full size. Giant wedding iris is a dramatic outlier among the African irises, a critically endangered species restricted in the wild to Lord Howe Island off the Australian coast, where it grows into a massive, coarse-textured clump of broad, leathery, sword-like leaves that can reach six feet or more, far exceeding the mainland African Dietes species in every dimension. Tall branching stems rise well above the foliage bearing large, white, iris-like flowers marked with yellow and soft mauve at the base of the falls, opening in flushes through much of the year in frost-free climates. Because it comes from a mild, humid, oceanic island climate, it is markedly more cold-sensitive than the South African fortnight lilies and is best reserved for true tropical and warm-subtropical gardens, where its bold scale makes it a striking specimen or accent plant near water features and courtyards.

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in sharply drained, sandy soil in full sun; keep completely dry through the summer dormant season to prevent the corms from rotting.

directions: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in sharply drained, sandy soil in full sun, then keep the corms completely dry through their summer dormancy, since rot in wet summer soil is the most common cause of failure with this species. One of the rarest of the Cape moraeas and now critically endangered in its tiny native range on the sandy flats near Cape Town, it produces a single narrow leaf and short stems bearing large, luminous, sky-blue flowers marked on each of the three outer tepals with a bold, dark blue-black eye-spot ringed in iridescent blue-green, a dramatic target pattern that has made it a prized subject for specialist bulb collectors growing rare South African irids. As with other winter-rainfall moraeas, individual flowers last only a single day but a well-grown clump produces a succession of blooms over several weeks in late winter and early spring. Because habitat loss has made the wild population nearly extinct, plants and seed in cultivation represent an important conservation resource and should be grown from reputable specialist bulb sources only.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 1-2 inches deep in fall in sharply drained, sandy soil in full sun to light shade; keep dry during summer dormancy.

directions: Plant bulbs 1-2 inches deep in fall in sharply drained, sandy soil in full sun to light shade, then water regularly through the winter growing season and withhold water completely once the foliage yellows in late spring. Changeable Cape cowslip earns its name from the way its densely packed spike of tubular, sweetly fragrant flowers shifts color from top to bottom and as each bloom ages, opening in shades of dusty blue and violet at the tip of the spike while the older, lower flowers fade to yellow-brown, giving a single spike two or three distinct color zones at once. The narrow, often faintly spotted leaves emerge in autumn well ahead of the late-winter flower spikes. Like its more commonly grown relative Lachenalia aloides, it is a compact, easy pot subject for a bright, cool windowsill or unheated greenhouse in climates outside its hardiness range, and it rewards a strict dry summer rest with a more vigorous return the following season.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 1-2 inches deep in early fall in sharply drained, sandy soil in full sun; this is one of the earliest lachenalias to flower and benefits from being planted slightly earlier than later-blooming species.

directions: Plant bulbs 1-2 inches deep in early autumn in sharply drained, sandy soil in full sun, since redflower Cape cowslip is among the first lachenalias into growth and bloom each season, often flowering as early as late autumn to midwinter where summers are dry. The narrow, sometimes faintly maroon-spotted leaves are topped by dense spikes of small, tubular, sweetly scented flowers in deep wine-red to dusky pink shades, a richer and darker color range than the yellow-and-orange tones typical of the better-known Lachenalia aloides. As with other Cape cowslips, strict summer dryness is essential once the foliage dies back, making this an excellent candidate for a sunny, cool windowsill or bulb frame in climates where it cannot be left in the ground year-round. Its early bloom time makes it a valuable addition for gardeners wanting to extend the Cape bulb season before the main flush of winter-growing lachenalias, babianas, and ixias begins.
